newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian opposition calls for daily protests.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian opposition calls for daily protests.

text.p: Bulgarian opposition protesters determined to break the ex-communist ruling party's grip on power clashed with police on Saturday after security forces broke up a 10-hour siege of parliament.
An opposition leader said crisis talks between President Zhelyu Zhelev and political and security chiefs, including opposition leaders, had ended without agreement.
Yordan Sokolov, parliamentary leader of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), said opposition leaders might no longer be able to control protests.
UDF chief Ivan Kostov called for daily protests until the Socialists agreed to the opposition's demand for general elections but urged the crowds to keep away from parliament.
Scuffles broke out outside the presidency as Zhelev's meeting with government and opposition politicians and security chiefs began.
Riot police used clubs to break up a 10-hour opposition siege of parliament early on Saturday in the worst violence in the country since the collapse of one-party communist rule.
Zhelev said he would not ask the Socialists to form a new government on Saturday as expected, but the ruling party appeared determined to complete its parliamentary term.
State news agency BTA quoted Krassimir Premyanov, head of the Socialists' parliamentary group, as saying the party would not give up its mandate.
Large crowds gathered outside Sofia's gold-domed cathedral, traditional rallying point for the opposition, waiting for opposition leaders to give the results of the meeting.

"For the first time we are proud that we are Bulgarians, that the whole world is watching us. We hope that we will do even better than our brothers the Serbs," said Dimitar Trifonov, 33, referring to eight weeks of protests against the Socialist government in Belgrade.
Anti-terrorist forces surrounded parliament and interior ministry troop reinforcements were arriving. Police vehicles full of dogs were parked nearby, among the debris, broken glass and smashed cars.
Protests were held in half a dozen Bulgarian cities on Friday. BTA said local authorities in the Lovec region, which groups four large provincial towns, had banned mass gatherings.

Many protesters brought children to the cathedral, despite the violence of yesterday's clashes. "If anything happens we will go into the church," said one woman with a young son, referring to a tradition dating from Ottoman rule.

Zhelev met the army chief, the defence minister, the speaker of parliament, the acting foreign minister, the heads of parties' parliamentary groups, outgoing prime minister Zhan Videnov and Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, the Socialists' nominee for premier.

"We believe that the president must not give the Socialists a mandate to form a new government because the situation is explosive. This situation cannot be resolved without early elections and the Socialists know this," said Yordan Sokolov, head of the UDF parliamentary group.

The confrontation, spurred by acute economic crisis, came after the governing Socialist Party refused to vote on Friday on a motion calling for fresh elections. The UDF walked out and urged a nationwide strike and civil disobedience.

What began with a human chain around the parliament building on Friday turned into a siege, trapping Socialist deputies inside. The demonstrators broke windows in the parliament and smashed and overturned cars which deputies had parked outside.
In the early hours of Saturday the police moved in using clubs and firing blank cartridges to beat a path into the parliament and allow the Socialist deputies out.

BTA said 97 people were injured, including 85 civilians, among them two UDF deputies, four security guards from parliament and eight police. Former UDF prime minister Filip Dimitrov needed surgery for a head injury.

Outgoing foreign minister Georgi Pirinski met ambassadors from Europe, the United States and Russia to explain the situation. The International Monetary Fund and World Bank have suspended new funding because of Bulgaria's reluctance to carry out badly-needed economic reforms.
